processing: Standard sheng pu-erh: sun-dried maocha, kept loose or pressed, with no ripe-style fermentation.
harvest_season: Not documented for this tea; in Yibang as elsewhere in Xishuangbanna, the spring picking is the prized one.
appearance_dry: As is typical of Yibang, smaller and finer leaf than big-leaf Yunnan tea, in dark-green strands with pale buds.
appearance_liquor: In young tea, typically clear pale gold.
appearance_wet: Typically small to medium, tender olive-green leaves.
taste_profile: Little is documented about this tea on its own. Yibang tea in general is described as refined, smooth and floral, with notable sweetness and a clean, lingering sweet return.

brewing.notes: Small Yibang leaf infuses quickly. Water just off the boil and short steeps suit it, as they do other fine-leaved Yibang tea.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, like other sheng, mainly as old-tree spring tea in small lots. A published spring price index listed old-tree leaf at 5,000 to 8,000 yuan per kilogram, well above many mountain names. At that level a clear statement of plot and year matters.
description:
Mao'erduo means cat's ear, and it is a name used for tea from Yibang, one of the six old tea mountains in Mengla County. What exactly it covers is hardly written down: it is unclear from the record whether it marks a plot or a leaf type, and it would be a guess to say the name describes the leaf.

Yibang stands out in Yunnan because many of its trees are medium- and small-leaved, not big-leaved, which pushes the tea toward a finer, more delicate style. The tea is made by normal sheng methods.

As with other Yibang tea, expect sweetness and smoothness over power. Brew with short steeps, since the small leaf gives itself up quickly.

This is an expensive name with little public documentation, so ask the seller directly what Mao'erduo means for their tea and where it was picked.
history:
Yibang was an administrative centre in the Qing dynasty and a main source of tribute pu-erh. War and the upheavals of the twentieth century damaged its gardens, and its reputation was rebuilt from the 2000s. A story that its small-leaf trees were introduced from Sichuan centuries ago is unconfirmed.

The name Mao'erduo itself has no documented early history; it appears mainly in modern price lists and tea trade writing.
